title: When You’re Speaking to Students, Speak Your Best (Plus a Primer on How We Learn to Read) -we-learn-to-read/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. starts from a 2020 study linking the syntactic complexity of preschool and kindergarten teachers' speech to students' vocabulary growth. He cautions that one study is only one study, and urges teachers to avoid reflexive cynicism about research by asking which research and which studies. He then connects the finding to the older evidence that listening comprehension outpaces reading comprehension until middle school, and to the Simple View of Reading, in which comprehension is word recognition multiplied by language comprehension. This frames why knowledge-rich elementary curricula and systematic decoding instruction both matter, and why a teacher cannot fix that alone. His practical takeaway is something teachers do control: using richer, more complex language with students every day, at no extra cost.
points: Teacher syntax complexity was associated with student vocabulary growth in a peer-reviewed study, which deserves serious but cautious attention.
Listening comprehension runs ahead of reading comprehension through the K-8 years, so read-alouds and knowledge-rich listening lessons should be emphasized early.
The Simple View of Reading is multiplicative, so weak decoding or weak background knowledge can each drive comprehension toward zero.
Teachers can choose to model elevated, varied language while still staying clear and concise.
quotes: First of all, one study is just one study. If subsequent studies replicate the findings of this one, then we’ll have a stronger sense of whether teacher syntax is something we all ought to start working on.

In other words, our K-8 students are going to tend to have maximum comprehension of complex language through listening rather than through reading. This doesn’t mean everything becomes a read-aloud now — but it does mean that knowledge-rich curricula in the elementary grades ought to heavily emphasize listening and learning lessons (e.g., read-alouds), slowly incorporating an increasing amount of the reading of complex texts as children progress through school.

Importantly, there is a multiplicative relationship between the two factors — and when you multiply by zero, you get zero. When a reader has weak word recognition skills, then so much of the mind’s resources will be spent on simply trying to discern the words on the page that even the richest background knowledge will not help with reading comprehension.

Yet if a child has perfect word recognition skills and can read aloud a complex text in my class with perfect fluency and prosody, but that child has weak background knowledge on the text’s topic and a poor grip on academic and domain-specific vocabulary, then guess what? The child will struggle to comprehend.

We can choose to use the full extent of our vocabulary when we work with students: one-on-one, small group, whole class. We can choose to learn new words and incorporate them into how we talk. We still shoot for clarity and concision when we instruct — when you confuse you lose!* — but we aim at elevating our language.

It costs us nothing extra. We’re already giving instruction, working with small groups, conferring with students and so on. Let’s take this study in Early Childhood Research Quarterly as an indicator that we might as well model our best speaking and language use as we do so.
